newsitem.title: ITALY: FEATURE - Italian justice in dock as investigations multiply.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Italian justice in dock as investigations multiply.

text.p: Italy's slow-paced justice system has many of the ingredients of popular soap operas -- high drama, intrigue and a plot that runs and runs.

But recent twists, introducing star magistrates who have begun to investigate each other for alleged graft rather than hound corrupt politicians and industrialists, have left Italians wondering whose hand is writing the storyline.

"People have believed in the judges rather than politicians up until now, and I think with reason," said leftist senator Giovanni Pellegrino, who has criticised magistrates as having a "strategic design" and being hungry for political power.
"But even their confidence in the judges will collapse as an effect of all this legal action."

The latest investigation -- into the hugely popular former anti-graft magistrate and ex-minister Antonio Di Pietro -- has threatened the credibility of the very people who exposed corruption at the core of Italian public life.
"Even the judicial powers, who seemed immune to Italy's crises, have not remained unharmed," said Nicola Mancino, speaker of the upper house of parliament, the Senate.
OPERATION CLEAN HANDS -- A REVOLUTION GONE WRONG?

For almost five years, a new breed of independent young magistrates -- dubbed the "Clean Hands" pool -- exposed a cosy web of corruption at the heart of Italian politics and business to which the law had previously turned a blind eye.
The revolution that blew open Italy's Tangentopoli (Bribesville) scandal seemingly spared no one.

At least 19 senior politicians have been investigated or sent to court in the past three years, including former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi, a defendant in two corruption trials, and Prime Minister Romano Prodi, whom Rome prosecutors want to try for alleged business malpractice.
Top figures in business, including Cesare Romiti, head of Italy's flagship firm Fiat, are also on trial or face probes.

Magistrates uncovered a fresh scandal in September, immediately nicknamed "Tangentopoli 2", in which an alleged super-lobby of businessmen, judges and lawyers paid bribes to win contracts or fix trials.

A prominent banker arrested during the latest investigation cast a shadow over the entire Clean Hands operation when he charged that Di Pietro, who quit as public works minister last month, had used less than correct working methods.

Now that Di Pietro himself is under investigation by magistrates to see if he really was the "Mr Clean" that Italians love, many are questioning whether the revolution that he symbolised is in danger of falling apart.
WHAT NEXT?
Prodi and members of his centre-left government, which took office six months ago with a promise to renew Italy from top to bottom, have stayed aloof from the investigations.

But the current state of tension, which centre-right leader Berlusconi calls a "judicial emergency", has prompted Justice Minister Giovanni Maria Flick to tell magistrates they should stick to their jobs and stay out of politics.
Some politicians and commentators argue that the way to close Tangentopoli and the judicial problems it has sparked is an amnesty, at least for illegal party financing.
"If a damaging phenomenon like Tangentopoli has been able to grow to the extent we have seen, there's a simple reason," life senator Leo Valiani told news magazine L'Espresso.
"The state has been, and still is, too weak...(An amnesty) can be an act of strength if it is intended as a point of departure for a more efficient justice system."
Magistrates want stricter laws to help stamp out administrative cheating and combat corruption effectively, as well as changes to the penal code and a faster system.
"It's above all outside the law courts that the problem of corruption will be resolved," said Gherardo Colombo, an assistant Milan prosecutor and member of the Clean Hands pool.
REFORM OF THE LAW
Reform of the law promises to be highly politically sensitive, given the current investigations.

Flick, a trained lawyer, has drafted a series of reforms to go before parliament designed to safeguard the independence of the judiciary while making more use of plea-bargaining and speeding up Italy's painstakingly slow court system.
Antonio Padoa Schioppa, head of the law faculty at Milan university, said that was "the primary emergency".
"The cancer of Italian justice is its slowness," he said.

Some 1,000 people have been sentenced since Tangentopoli broke in February 1992 but under Italian law, a sentence becomes final only once the full appeals process has been exhausted -- and that takes literally years.

"It will take until the third millennium to know whether Andreotti is guilty or innocent," said Padoa Schioppa, referring to seven-times prime minister Giulio Andreotti who is accused of protecting the Mafia and ordering a political killing.
"By the time you arrive at a final decision in Italy, the defendant is either already dead or almost dead. It's scandalous."
